## Problem

You are given a list of messages, where each message is represented as a triplet: `[<sender>, <receiver>, <message>]`. For any given sender-receiver pair, if the sender transmits multiple messages to that same receiver, those messages are treated as **duplicates (spam)**.

Your goal is to determine the top `k` receivers who have obtained the most **unique (non-spam)** messages. A unique message is defined by a distinct sender-receiver pair—multiple messages from the same sender to the same receiver count only once. If there is a tie in the count of unique messages, the receivers should be ranked alphabetically (lexicographically smaller names come first).

**Constraints:**
- `k` will never exceed the total number of unique receivers.
- Duplicate messages from the same sender to the same receiver must be counted as a single unique message.
- When two or more receivers share the same count, the one with the lexicographically smaller name is considered higher ranked.

**Example 1:**
> **Input:** messages = [
>   ["Jack", "Mary", "I love you"],
>   ["Jack", "Mary", "I miss you"],
>   ["Jack", "Rose", "Hello"],
>   ["Alice", "Mary", "Are you available"],
>   ["Bob", "Rose", "Hi there"],
>   ["John", "Lisa", "Hi there"],
>   ["John", "Lisa", "Hi there!"],
>   ["John", "Lisa", "Hi there!!"],
>   ["John", "Lisa", "Hi there!!!"]
> ], k = 2
> **Output:** ["Mary", "Rose"]
> **Explanation:**
> - "Mary" receives unique messages from "Jack" and "Alice" (count = 2).
> - "Rose" receives unique messages from "Jack" and "Bob" (count = 2).
> - "Lisa" only receives messages from "John" (count = 1).
>
> Since "Mary" and "Rose" tie with a count of 2, the lexicographically smaller name "Mary" is placed first.

**Example 2:**
> **Input:** messages = [
>   ["Jack", "Mary", "I love you"],
>   ["Jack", "Rose", "I miss you"],
>   ["Jack", "Alice", "Let's have dinner tonight"],
>   ["Alice", "Mary", "Are you available"]
> ], k = 2
> **Output:** ["Mary", "Alice"]

**Example 3:**
> **Input:** messages = [
>   ["Jack", "Mary", "Hello"],
>   ["Alice", "Rose", "Good morning"],
>   ["Jack", "Mary", "Hi"],
>   ["Alice", "Rose", "Good afternoon"],
>   ["Bob", "Tom", "Hi Tom"],
>   ["Jack", "Mary", "Hey"],
>   ["Charlie", "Tom", "Hello Tom"],
>   ["Charlie", "Jack", "Hello Jack"]
> ], k = 3
> **Output:** ["Tom", "Jack", "Mary"]

## Hints

<details>
<summary>Hint 1</summary>

Collapse repeated sender-receiver pairs before counting, the message content is not what makes a message unique.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2</summary>

Use a hash set per receiver to deduplicate senders, then count the set sizes.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3</summary>

After counting, select the top k receivers with a heap or partial sort, define tie-breaking if the problem requires it.

</details>
